paper.title: Xolver: Multi-Agent Reasoning with Holistic Experience Learning Just Like an Olympiad Team
paper.central_claim: Xolver, a training-free multi-agent framework with a persistent evolving memory (episodic corpus plus per-query shared memory), judge and tools, consistently outperforms specialized reasoning agents and often larger models on math and coding benchmarks.

provenance.notes: actual_model/session_id/receipt_ref null: the Agent tool result exposes no per-call receipt to the worker; model_type is the configured slot (agent_model=haiku -> claude-sonnet-5-5[1m]) as assigned by the controller.

sections_read: Appendix B qualitative examples (one math, one code)

evidence.quote: a training-free, multi-agent reasoning framework that equips a black-box LLM with a persistent, evolving memory of holistic experience
evidence.support_explanation: Central claim framing; training-free means the retained object is non-weight memory.

evidence.quote: they standalone each problem instance, generating solutions from scratch without accumulating or transferring insights from rich, diverse experiential knowledge.
evidence.support_explanation: Author gap statement.

evidence.quote: can also be updated with UpdateEpisodicMemory by adding the top-ranked reasoning and response
evidence.support_explanation: Write rule: the top-ranked entry of the per-problem shared memory is appended to the external corpus; no threshold, dedup or retirement is described.

evidence.quote: the shared memory facilitates knowledge transfer between agents and across iterations
evidence.support_explanation: The shared memory is a per-query top-m store, discarded after the query; the persistent part is only the episodic corpus.

evidence.quote: reflects an LLM-estimated correctness probability
evidence.support_explanation: Math scores that rank entries and decide what is written are LLM-estimated, not verified.

evidence.quote: test case outcomes are determined by simulating execution through LLM prompting within the judge agent
evidence.support_explanation: For code the in-loop test outcomes are LLM-simulated rather than executed.

evidence.quote: we use accuracy using GPT-4o
evidence.support_explanation: Math final-answer accuracy is judged with GPT-4o; code uses pass@1.

evidence.quote: we report the average accuracy and pass@1 metric, calculated by averaging 32 inference runs for competitive benchmarks LiveCodeBench and AIME ’25 , and 16 runs for AIME ’24
evidence.support_explanation: Repeated runs for the hard benchmarks (Table 4 reports mean and std).

evidence.quote: using a single greedy-decoded generation
evidence.support_explanation: GSM8K and Math-500 are single-run.

evidence.quote: for model-based baselines (a–c), we report official results from their technical reports or corresponding benchmark leaderboards
evidence.support_explanation: Model baselines are not rerun under the same protocol; agent baselines are rerun with the same backbone (previous clause).

evidence.quote: For math, we use the OpenMathReason dataset
evidence.support_explanation: External retrieval corpus for math; no overlap audit with GSM8K / Math-500 / AIME is reported.

evidence.locator: Sec 3.2 Main Results (Effectiveness of Dynamic Episodic Memory)
evidence.quote: On average, episodic memory integration yields a +3.5 point improvement across both backbones and datasets where the largest gain is +7.7 points with o3-mini-medium on coding (LiveCodeBench).
evidence.support_explanation: Retention effect: Xolver(+) with cross-problem write-back vs Xolver(-) with static episodic memory.

evidence.quote: and from 66.3 to 79.6 on LiveCodeBench
evidence.support_explanation: Text attributes the (+) variant with 79.6 but Table 1 lists 79.6 for Xolver(-) and 87.3 for (+); a reporting inconsistency.

evidence.quote: Each component plays a necessary role, with the most significant degradation observed when removing Multi-iteration and Multi-Agent followed by Judge Agent
evidence.support_explanation: Component ablation (values in Fig 3, not in text): the largest drops come from iteration/multi-agent, i.e. from test-time compute structure rather than from stored experience.

evidence.quote: we conduct a budget-controlled experiment on the AIME ’25 dataset
evidence.support_explanation: Budget-matched agents x iterations analysis; shows structure helps beyond raw budget.

evidence.quote: self-judging agents tend to be biased in favor of their own outputs, occasionally validating incorrect solutions
evidence.support_explanation: Evidence that judge independence matters; also a risk because the judge decides what enters memory.

evidence.quote: we conduct an ablation study by randomly shuffling the sequence of problems in each task
evidence.support_explanation: Order-sensitivity control for the online write-back (Appendix D.3, 5 runs, std about 1).

evidence.quote: due to its collaborative and iterative multi-agent reasoning
evidence.support_explanation: Higher cost than a single-agent baseline (about 1.5x Search-o1 in tokens, per Fig 8 text) is acknowledged.

evidence.quote: average performance with multiple trials
evidence.support_explanation: Mean and std over 16/32 runs; Xolver(+) std 0.2-0.7, Xolver(-) up to 1.3.

evidence.quote: faces limitations in computational efficiency, with substantially higher token consumption than traditional approaches
evidence.support_explanation: Author-stated cost limitation.

evidence.quote: which dynamically updates the episodic memory after solving each problem to utilize accumulated knowledge across problems
evidence.support_explanation: Definition of Xolver(+): in-competition write-back on the evaluated problems.

evidence.quote: a dynamic benchmark that ensures no data leakage by periodically releasing new problems
evidence.support_explanation: Author claim for LiveCodeBench; the code corpus is a 9M-token cp-algorithms collection, not audited against v5 problems.

evidence.quote: remain confined to single-agent architectures
evidence.support_explanation: Closest neighbors (CheatSheet, Search-o1) are positioned by agent count; both are run as baselines.

evidence.quote: despite the latter relying on costly per-problem memory updates
evidence.support_explanation: CheatSheet is the nearest cross-problem memory baseline; cost argument is made, equal-budget comparison is not.

evidence.quote: tool usage remains decoupled from the model’s core reasoning process
evidence.support_explanation: Author-observed failure: tools are not reliably invoked.

evidence.quote: Accuracy improves consistently with more agents and iterations, reflecting the benefits of experience accumulation, though at increased cost.
evidence.support_explanation: Interpretation conflates test-time compute scaling with experience accumulation.

signatures.object: external episodic corpus D_E (past problem, reasoning trace, solution) that conditions all agents at iteration 0; static for Xolver(-), written back for Xolver(+)
signatures.information: problem text only; reasoning traces optional; judge scores; no gold labels
signatures.operation: BM25 retrieve top-K examples (K=5 in analysis) as context; after solving, append the top-ranked (problem, trace, response) from the shared memory
signatures.output: examples injected into the first-iteration context of every dynamic agent
signatures.conditions: m=3 agents, 2 iterations, temperature 0.2; self-retrieval from model parametric memory when no corpus
signatures.feedback: LLM judge score (math: estimated correctness; code: LLM-simulated test outcomes over given plus 10 synthesized tests)
signatures.selection_rule: highest judge score in the shared memory; no minimum score, dedup or retirement
signatures.persistence: corpus grows over the test stream in (shuffled-checked) order
signatures.later_use: later problems in the same benchmark
signatures.failure_boundary: self-judge bias; wrong-but-top-ranked solutions can be written back

signatures.object: per-problem multi-agent inference scaffold (planner-chosen roles, judge, per-query shared memory, verifier/debugger)
signatures.information: problem, own prior thoughts, judge feedback, top-m shared entries
signatures.operation: iterate agents -> judge -> keep top-m -> repeat until convergence or limit -> extract answer
signatures.claimed_effect: largest ablation drops from multi-iteration and multi-agent

gap.author_gap: LLM reasoning treats every problem as an isolated attempt; prior experience-augmentation methods cover one modality each (retrieval, tools, or multi-agent), so no system accumulates a combined repertoire.
gap.checked_gap: The isolation premise is addressed by CheatSheet and Search-o1-style cross-problem memory, which Xolver runs as baselines; the actual residual (what holistic integration buys over the best single-modality memory) is only shown through aggregate comparison, and the paper itself shows most gain comes from iteration/multi-agent structure.

multi-agent reasoning: CAMEL, AgentVerse, AutoGen, DyLAN, CodeSim
tool-augmented reasoning: PAL, ReAct, Chameleon, OctoTools

gap.method_response: Unified scaffold with episodic corpus, per-query shared memory, judge, verifier and Python tool.
gap.remaining_gap: Compute-matched comparison, contamination audit, write gating, frozen vs growing corpus on unseen sets.

assessment.strongest_supported_claim: A judge-driven multi-agent scaffold lifts reasoning benchmarks well above the same backbone and reproduced agent baselines, and writing solved problems back to an episodic corpus adds a further 3-8 points in-stream; holistic experience learning as the driver is not isolated.

Wrong-answer write-back and judge bias effect on later problems

G.reason: Real limitation (no cross-problem experience in single-pass reasoning) but nearest neighbours (CheatSheet, Search-o1, Reflexion) already address it and run as baselines; the claimed gap of unifying modalities is integration-level, and the paper shows most gains come from iteration/agent structure.

M.reason: Mechanism is explicit with algorithm and prompts, separates per-query refinement from persistent episodic memory, and yields testable predictions (self-judge bias, order sensitivity, agents x iterations at fixed budget) that were run; judge reliability for writes remains weak.

X.reason: Inference loop fully specified, but retention is a bare append of the top-judged entry with LLM-estimated correctness or LLM-simulated tests: no admission threshold, dedup, versioning, retirement or rollback.

E.measurement.reason: Code uses benchmark tests; math uses GPT-4o-judged accuracy with no validation; model baselines are copied from reports; in-loop judging is LLM-based; Table 1 text/number mismatch noted (E013).

E.causality.reason: Same-backbone agent baselines, (+)/(-), external/self/no retrieval, component removals, self-judge and shuffle ablations, plus a budget-controlled study; missing equal-token self-consistency baseline and a wrong-entry write-back control.

E.holdout.reason: LiveCodeBench v5 and AIME25 are recent and order was shuffled 5 times, but (+) writes back evaluated problems, no overlap audit of OpenMathReason / cp-algorithms against test sets, and defaults m=3, I=2 have no stated selection data.

E.statistics.reason: 16/32-run means with std for AIME/LiveCodeBench and 5-run shuffle std, large effect sizes versus small std; GSM8K/Math-500 single-run, baselines without variance, no significance test.

E.cost.reason: Token breakdown by dataset, about 1.5x Search-o1, complexity O(mI) tokens vs O(I) runtime, limitation acknowledged, and a fixed-budget agents x iterations study; headline comparisons are not compute-matched and no dollar cost.

rationale: Strong, well-ablated inference scaffold with multi-run variance and a (+)/(-) retention contrast; the retained episodic write-back is ungated and unaudited, most gain comes from per-query compute structure, and compute is unmatched.
